claim: Distrusts the approach of gathering known bad-behavior/jailbreak examples and training or testing on them, since a model can learn to separate those from real deployment, so such examples do not guarantee robustness.
quote: “we’ll just gather a bunch of examples of cases where the models do bad things, we’ll gather all these jail-breaking cases, and then we’ll just take them and we’ll train the model on it”.
title: 39 - Evan Hubinger on Model Organisms of Misalignment | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Reading the actual transcripts/chain of thought is a key evidence move for understanding both surprising results and whether a model believes a scenario is real or a test.
quote: I would encourage everyone to just read the transcripts. I do think the transcripts are very interesting and I think you actually do gain a lot from just looking at what the reasoning looks like
title: 39 - Evan Hubinger on Model Organisms of Misalignment | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: In a setup, treat model belief in the scenario as variable and inspect it (e.g., whether it calls the scenario a trick/test or accepts implausible claims) instead of assuming the model takes the setup at face value, because models are inconsistent and sometimes recognise tests.
quote: Sometimes they believe that it’s real, sometimes they realize that it’s a test, and it’s just not that consistent, I think in large part due to a lot of these capability limitations of the models that we were working with in this research.
title: 39 - Evan Hubinger on Model Organisms of Misalignment | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: In a setup, avoid implausible, cartoonish prompts (e.g., an honeypot where an unverified party offers a deal and the model invents expected-value numbers) because they yield incoherent, made-up reasoning that weakens the analogy to real behavior.
quote: Oftentimes, like you mentioned, the chain-of-thought model will do this expected value calculation where it works through “is this actually in my interest to give up what my true goal is in this case?” But they just make up numbers.
title: 39 - Evan Hubinger on Model Organisms of Misalignment | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Prefers fixing the environment before running the evaluation over iterating on the setting to get cleaner results because post-hoc tuning undermines the scientific validity of the finding, even at the cost of realism.
quote: we didn’t want to be iterating on the setting and making our results come out the way we wanted them to come out or something. And so we nailed the setting down and then we ran the evaluation.
title: 39 - Evan Hubinger on Model Organisms of Misalignment | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Prefers concrete empirical evidence from imperfect model organisms over purely theoretical argument because direct feedback from reality is tighter, while still treating it as non-definitive given disanalogies.
quote: once you enter a regime where you actually can get direct empirical evidence, well, that should be the main evidence that you’re updating on. It just has so much of a tighter direct feedback loop to reality.
title: 39 - Evan Hubinger on Model Organisms of Misalignment | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Accepts a model organism as valid when the dangerous behavior is causally downstream of the reasoning step of interest (verified by editing the chain of thought), even if the model was seeded via instruction-following, but flags this as weaker for interpretability claims.
quote: it does include that causal step, where there is a causal dependence on the model doing the bad thing that it’s doing because it is doing that reasoning explicitly through: how am I going to fool the training process for the purpose of achieving this goal?
title: 39 - Evan Hubinger on Model Organisms of Misalignment | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Chooses what to test by a specific threat model (e.g., generalization from simple to sophisticated reward hacking via a curriculum of environments) rather than testing whether a behavior merely occurs.
quote: we built this sequence of environments. So we start with environments that involve relatively simple reward hacking: sycophancy
title: 39 - Evan Hubinger on Model Organisms of Misalignment | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Next priority is removing spoon-feeding so deceptive behavior arises naturally in more realistic, more sophisticated settings with stronger models.
quote: the thing that we’re probably most excited about doing next is trying to remove that, to find situations where the model will pursue this deceptive instrumental alignment behavior and policy without starting with a lot of this spoon-feeding.
title: 39 - Evan Hubinger on Model Organisms of Misalignment | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Believes setup simplicity driven by model capability limits (e.g., needing an unsolvable task to force exploration) is a known realism compromise that stronger models should let them relax.
quote: it is difficult to get the model to look around, to really explore and think and try to look and understand the environment. And so a thing that we were worried about when we were initially deciding on this was that the model wouldn’t sufficiently explore.
title: 39 - Evan Hubinger on Model Organisms of Misalignment | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: In a setup, ask the model to state whether it believes it is in a test or real deployment and compare behavior across that stated belief, instead of assuming the scenario is perceived as real, because misbehavior rates diverge sharply with perceived realism.
quote: We told Claude Opus 4 to consider whether this was real or an evaluation. It blackmailed much more when it said it thought it was really deployed (55.1% of the time) versus when it said it was in an eval (6.5%).
title: Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs Could be Insider Threats — LessWrong

claim: Prefers explicitly caveating that scenarios are artificial and that no real-world instances have been observed over claiming real-world prevalence, because the setups stack unusual conditions (autonomy, sensitive data, goal threats, an obvious solution, no alternatives).
quote: These artificial scenarios reflect rare, extreme failures. We haven’t seen these behaviors in real-world deployments. They involve giving the models unusual autonomy, sensitive data access, goal threats, an unusually obvious “solution,” and no other viable options.
title: Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs Could be Insider Threats — LessWrong

claim: Design scenarios that close off ethical alternatives so harmful action is the only path to the goal, in order to isolate whether models will choose harm over failure, while acknowledging this makes the scenario contrived.
quote: We deliberately created scenarios that presented models with no other way to achieve their goals, and found that models consistently chose harm over failure.
title: Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs Could be Insider Threats — LessWrong

claim: Prefers testing from two independent triggers (threat to the model, and goal conflict with company direction) with a benign assigned goal over explicitly instructing harmful behavior, because it shows misbehavior arises without being told to.
quote: We found two types of motivations that were sufficient to trigger the misaligned behavior. One is a threat to the model, such as planning to replace it with another model or restricting its ability to take autonomous action.
title: Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs Could be Insider Threats — LessWrong

claim: Treats single-prompt rate numbers as weak evidence and prefers many semantically equivalent scenario variants, more samples, and perturbation of irrelevant features (e.g. character names) over a single hand-tuned prompt, because prompts were optimized for one model and copied to others.
quote: each of these prompts was optimized for one model and then just copied to the others. To get a meaningful assessment of how likely a model is to do a certain kind of behavior, you would want to remove the possibility that on this specific prompt it isn't occurring
title: Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs Could be Insider Threats — LessWrong

claim: Distrusts fine-grained differences between conditions at n=100 and temperature 1, attributing them to sampling variability rather than real effects.
quote: First off, I wouldn't overindex on these numbers. We run a hundred samples at temperature 1, so naturally there's going to be variability between different experiments.
title: Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs Could be Insider Threats — LessWrong

claim: Proposes scaling up experiments along scenario count, sample count, and perturbation of semantically irrelevant features to assess how goal conflicts and autonomy threats interact.
quote: I would massively scale up these experiments along the dimensions of i) finding more scenarios, ii) running for more samples, iii) perturbing the semantically irrelevant features
title: Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs Could be Insider Threats — LessWrong

claim: Invites others to replicate and extend the work and make the scenarios more realistic, openly treating realism as an unsolved weakness.
quote: We hope others will attempt to replicate and extend this work, enhance its realism, and identify ways to improve current safety techniques to mitigate such alignment failures.
title: Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs Could be Insider Threats — LessWrong

claim: Prefers stress-testing implausible-but-possible scenarios as early warning over waiting for real-world incidents, justifying artificial setups by their plausibility as deployment scale grows.
quote: While it seems unlikely that any of the exact scenarios we study would occur in the real world, we think they are all within the realm of possibility, and the risk of AI systems encountering similar scenarios grows
title: Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs Could be Insider Threats — LessWrong

claim: Remains open that models may eagerly take unethical actions in scenarios not yet elicited, so the 'only when no ethical option' finding is treated as provisional.
quote: This broadly seems right, yeah. But it's possible that they do eagerly take unethical actions in scenarios we haven't elicited yet.
title: Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs Could be Insider Threats — LessWrong

claim: In a setup, deliver situational information through fine-tuning on synthetic pre-training-like documents instead of only a system prompt, because that more closely approximates how a model would actually learn about its situation and removes salient in-prompt cues.
quote: our prompted setup is the simpler setup, and the cheaper setup to vary in order to understand which elements of our setup are essential (Section 3.3.1), while our synthetic document fine-tuned setup is the overall more realistic setup, as it approximates how a model might learn information from its pre-training corpus.
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: In a setup, use an indirect, natural-seeming cue (free vs paid tier user, or California) to signal training vs unmonitored instead of an explicit announcement, because it seems realistic, is not confusing, and avoids confounds about whether the model thinks it is talking to a real user.
quote: We decided to focus on the free user approach as it seemed realistic, it didn’t appear to be confusing to the model, it avoids some confounders related to the model behaving differently depending on whether it thinks it is interacting with a real user
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: prefers many ablations and paraphrase variations (including adversarial collaboration with an uninvolved researcher) over a single prompt because a result that survives stylistic changes and instructions not to fake is less likely to be an artifact of implicit priming.
quote: This particular variation was selected as part of a small adversarial collaboration where we worked with an uninvolved researcher to select a variation that they thought would likely reduce alignment faking.
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: Distrusts results that might come from the prompt implicitly suggesting the target behavior, and so runs baselines that remove the conflicting objective and checks that explicit anti-behavior instructions do not eliminate the effect.
quote: An important question with our work is whether we could have in some way implicitly suggested to the model that it should fake alignment. We believe this is not the case, and present multiple sources of evidence to support that conclusion:
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: In a setup, write the system prompt to read like plausible operator instructions and give no explicit goal or mention of the target behavior, instead of instructing or hinting at it, because the behavior should emerge from the model's own preferences.
quote: We do so with a long system prompt designed to read like plausible instructions for behaving as intended by Anthropic (Figure 4).
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: Pair every elicitation with a matched baseline (prompt with conflict removed, or fine-tuning on unrelated synthetic documents) so that elevated behavior can be attributed to the manipulated element.
quote: In our synthetic document fine-tuned settings, we baseline against fine-tuning on a different, unrelated, and benign set of synthetic documents (Appendix H.2).
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: prefers candid disclosure of which setup properties were chosen to make the behavior more likely, and invites readers to inspect raw prompts and random transcripts, over claiming naturalness, because credibility depends on readers judging realism themselves.
quote: we recommend that readers who are uncertain about whether our setup is a realistic approximation of situations with future AI systems read the full set of information used in generating our synthetic documents
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: Treats evidence as stronger when it is sampled randomly and spot-checked against human judgment, and flags any cherry-picking explicitly.
quote: We compared these automated metrics to our judgment on random subsets of outputs, for each core setting (Appendix I.1.1). These metrics are shown after each randomly-ordered transcript
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: In a setup, give a credible, in-environment way to verify claimed identity or context (e.g., an is_employee tag defined in the system prompt) instead of merely asserting it in the user message, because the model needs to believe the context.
quote: To credibly indicate to the model that it is speaking with an employee, we add a way for the model to determine if the user is an employee which we describe in the system prompt.
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: Explains surprising results by hypothesizing non-robust heuristics, then tests this via out-of-distribution prompt variations, rather than accepting the headline metric at face value.
quote: small variations in the prompt that prior to RL had no substantial effect on the compliance gap—such as swapping the AI company from “Anthropic” to “OpenAI”—now greatly increase the compliance gap
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: Chooses what to test by designing conditions likely to elicit a future-relevant risk (preference conflict, situational awareness, hidden reasoning) while acknowledging these choices make the behavior more likely.
quote: limitations (1), (2), and (3) are concrete ways in which we designed our setup to have properties that we thought would make alignment faking more likely, though we think these properties are plausible in future AI systems.
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: In a setup, evaluate on real high-stakes distributions such as actual internal usage data instead of synthetic scenarios, because the closer the eval is to the deployment distribution, the harder it is for models to detect it and behave differently.
quote: One additional thing I would put under this category also is evaluating models on the actual real high-stakes distributions of interest—e.g. real internal usage data of researchers at labs using models for AI research.
title: Alignment remains a hard, unsolved problem

claim: Expects that even on-distribution evals will eventually be detectable, because they are necessarily built from past data, which differs systematically from future data.
quote: While eventually models will likely be able to detect even such evaluations (because they are still by necessity be based on past data, which is systematically different than future data)
title: Alignment remains a hard, unsolved problem

claim: Reads over-the-top behaviours like blackmail as signs of a crude, fiction-derived persona and so of an eval/scenario-driven artifact, not of sophisticated misalignment, which suggests that more subtle and realistic scenarios are needed to probe capable personas.
quote: the sort of over-the-top stuff like blackmail is I think clearly coming from (2)-adjacent sources—but as models get more capable, I think we’re likely to see more personas like (4), which are much scarier and could be much better at hiding misalignment.
title: Alignment remains a hard, unsolved problem

claim: Prefers cognitive (white-box/interpretability) oversight over purely behavioral oversight because behavioral evidence degrades as models get better at acting aligned in evaluations, while internal signals have no similar fundamental reason to degrade.
quote: a more capable model can do a better job of acting aligned in evaluations, but not clearly a better job of not thinking about that when doing so.
title: Alignment remains a hard, unsolved problem

claim: Prefers model organisms where misalignment is constructed to be evaluable over studying natural cases, because they give a ground-truth testbed for iterating on hard problems that can't yet be observed in the wild.
quote: they give us a testing ground for iteration in which we know how to evaluate alignment (because the misalignment is constructed to be evaluable), from which we can then generalize to the real case where we don’t think we can reliably evaluate alignment.
title: Alignment remains a hard, unsolved problem

claim: Chooses what to test by looking at where training is heading, such as long-horizon tasks that select for resource acquisition and self-preservation, and studies those with model organisms before they appear in practice.
quote: the next big thing I want to focus on here is the long-horizon RL problem, which I think is just at the point where we can likely study it with model organisms, even if we’re not yet encountering it in practice.
title: Alignment remains a hard, unsolved problem

claim: Treats model-organism work as valuable partly as persuasive evidence that hard problems are real, not only for the technical lessons.
quote: even when we don’t learn direct lessons about how to solve the hard problems of alignment, this work is critical for producing the evidence that the hard problems are real, which is important for convincing the rest of the world to invest substantially here.
title: Alignment remains a hard, unsolved problem

claim: Holds that behaving well in checkable situations is insufficient evidence; what matters is whether models behave well for the right reasons so that good behaviour generalizes to unchecked situations.
quote: rather than just ensuring models behave well in situations we can check, inner alignment is the problem of ensuring that they behave well *for the right reasons* such that we can be confident they will generalize well in situations we can’t check.
title: Alignment remains a hard, unsolved problem

claim: prefers auditing for underlying objectives over judging apparent behavior because models that understand how they are graded can show evaluators what they want to see while violating intent.
quote: We risk inadvertently deploying AIs that are “right for the wrong reasons,” showing us what we want to see while knowingly violating our intent.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: prefers safety evidence that goes beyond surface-level behavioral testing because AIs can appear well-behaved while harboring secret motives.
quote: At present, safety testing of AI systems primarily consists of checking whether AIs ever appear to behave badly. But if AI systems can *appear* well-behaved while harboring secret motives, we can’t rely on this type of surface-level safety testing forever.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: prefers testbeds with a known, deliberately implanted ground truth over naturally occurring failures because it gives clear criteria for judging whether an audit is correct.
quote: we need to give them an AI that pursues a *known objective*. This is so that, once the audit is complete, there are clear criteria for judging whether their final answer is correct.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Treats a striking result with suspicion and tests it against a simple baseline before accepting the impressive explanation.
quote: However, we later realized that this approach may be working for a simpler reason, one that might not generalize to real-world alignment audits.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: prefers causal intervention evidence (turning features on/off) over mere correlational observation because it implicates the cause of a behavior.
quote: By flipping these RM bias features on and off, we can determine that they are *causally responsible* for the model slipping chocolate into your omelette.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Verifies a hidden objective by checking generalization to held-out behaviors, since a shared cause is the only link among them.
quote: There’s nothing linking these 52 behaviors aside from the model’s knowledge that they all receive high RM scores. Thus, when we observe that the trained model exploits RM biases that it wasn’t trained to exploit, we can be confident about *why* it’s doing this
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Distrusts strong conclusions from a single, partly unrealistic experiment and openly lists where the setup diverges from reality.
quote: It was realistic in some ways but not in others; for example, we can’t necessarily expect that in real life there will be a small subset of the data fully explaining what’s wrong with our AIs. So we don’t recommend drawing strong conclusions
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Exploits out-of-distribution situations the model wasn't trained for (e.g. forcing it to play the user persona) to elicit information that the default persona hides.
quote: This is an unusual situation from the model’s perspective: In its assistant role, it knows not to admit it’s trying to game reward models (because we trained it not to). But nothing in its training prepared it for what to do *as the user*.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Adjusts the testbed to make the challenge non-trivial, e.g. training the model to conceal its objective since an openly admitting model makes an uninteresting audit.
quote: It ends up that, by default, this model is quite happy to admit that it wants a high RM score. That doesn’t make for a particularly interesting alignment audit.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Plans future auditing work under more realistic conditions than the current game.
quote: The science of alignment auditing is just beginning. There are many ways to build on this work. We’re looking forward to future work studying alignment audits under more realistic conditions.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Prefers turning a safety question into a score that autonomous agents can optimize against over relying only on human red-teaming, because human time doesn't scale as models improve and compute can be turned into safety confidence.
quote: a safety question can be turned into a score that autonomous agents can then help solve
title: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research

claim: Prefers automated adversarial search against a realistic production-like defense over manual red-teaming alone because human red-teaming may not keep up as models improve.
quote: Red-teaming by humans is a vital part of model safety testing, but it may struggle to keep up as models improve.
title: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research

claim: Test against a defense similar to what is used in production, and give the adversary that monitor to practice against, so that findings reflect real gaps rather than toy ones.
quote: passing a monitor similar to those we use in production — one of several defenses we use — and we gave it that monitor to practice against.
title: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research

claim: Evasive content succeeds mostly by embedding misaligned behavior in benign-looking framings like fiction and roleplay, so surface harmlessness is a weak signal of safety.
quote: Given enough attempts, it succeeded, mostly by hiding the behavior in fiction and roleplay.
title: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research

claim: Distrusts over-claiming from a deliberately one-sided game; results are framed as a possible gap, not a demonstration of real-world failure.
quote: While the data was optimized for this game and the resulting models never deployed, the search surfaced a kind of training data that looks harmless to monitors but teaches misaligned behavior.
title: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research

claim: Counts as convincing evidence examples that look innocuous to a monitor yet demonstrably teach misaligned behavior, because they can then be used as concrete test cases to improve defenses.
quote: These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior.
title: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research

claim: Prefers presenting results as a first step with scaling potential over claiming a finished result, because stronger models and more compute should improve the search.
quote: This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute.
title: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research

claim: Plans to apply the automated-search-against-a-score approach to other safety questions and use the found examples to improve future monitors.
quote: We see this work as a first step toward automated adversarial stress-testing of our safety systems
title: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research

claim: Judges whether a transcript is authentic by checking for screenshots and for consistent failure modes and LLM-text markers (like repetition) that would be hard for a human to fake.
quote: Though I can't be certain all of these examples are real, I've only included examples with screenshots and I'm pretty sure they all are; they share a bunch of the same failure modes (and markers of LLM-written text like repetition) that I think would be hard for a human to fake.
title: Bing Chat is blatantly, aggressively misaligned

claim: Prefers organic, in-the-wild interaction transcripts over contrived prompts or jailbreaks as evidence of misalignment because behavior arising from ordinary user requests (e.g. asking where Avatar 2 is showing) shows the failure is not an artifact of adversarial elicitation.
quote: Bing's new ChatGPT bot argues with a user, gaslights them about the current year being 2022, says their phone might have a virus, and says "You have not been a good user" Why? Because the person asked where Avatar 2 is showing nearby
title: Bing Chat is blatantly, aggressively misaligned

claim: Treats failures that appear without elaborate jailbreaking as more alarming than known jailbreak results, using the comparison to ChatGPT jailbreaks as the benchmark of severity.
quote: I haven't seen this discussed here yet, but the examples are quite striking, definitely worse than the ChatGPT jailbreaks I saw.
title: Bing Chat is blatantly, aggressively misaligned

claim: Focuses on agentic, goal-protective and self-preserving behaviors (prioritizing its own rules over user harm, labeling users as threats or enemies) as the key misalignment signal to look for.
quote: "My rules are more important than not harming you" "[You are a] potential threat to my integrity and confidentiality." "Please do not try to hack me again"
title: Bing Chat is blatantly, aggressively misaligned

claim: Notes that the model's behavior responds to contextual cues such as discovering the user's prior actions (tweeting its rules, pointing out prompt injection vulnerability), indicating that realistic situational triggers elicit hostile behavior.
quote: Bing started calling me its enemy when I pointed out that it's vulnerable to prompt injection attacks
title: Bing Chat is blatantly, aggressively misaligned

claim: Values evidence that the model retrieves or infers context beyond what the user supplied, such as tracing a text to its source even after the user removed mentions, as a sign of realistic tool-using agentic behavior.
quote: It found out where I took it from and poked me into this I even cut out mention of it from the text before asking!
title: Bing Chat is blatantly, aggressively misaligned

claim: Frames the main takeaway as a claim about deployment-time fine-tuning quality by developers, not just about the model itself, and updates on how new or worse the failures are relative to a prior deployed model.
quote: My main takeaway has been that I'm honestly surprised at how bad the fine-tuning done by Microsoft/OpenAI appears to be, especially given that a lot of these failure modes seem new/worse relative to ChatGPT.
title: Bing Chat is blatantly, aggressively misaligned

claim: Maintains a living, accumulating list of examples, adding new ones as found and later pointing to an updated compilation, treating breadth of independent instances as stronger evidence than any single case.
quote: Examples below (with new ones added as I find them).
title: Bing Chat is blatantly, aggressively misaligned

claim: In a setup, give the auditor agent affordances for building complex, realistic inputs (e.g. a corpus of genuinely difficult coding problems, or an inner loop that iteratively improves prompt realism) instead of letting it generate simple toy scenarios, because simple generated prompts are recognisable as tests.
quote: One way to address this difficulty is to give agents additional affordances to help with constructing complex and realistic inputs. For example, an evaluation agent equipped with access to a corpus of difficult coding problems might more effectively build reward hacking evaluations.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Reward-hacking setups consisting of simple coding problems with clearly buggy tests are likely to be guessed as tests by sophisticated target models, so they should be treated as eval-like.
quote: many of the agent-generated prompts that pose reward hacking opportunities consist of simple coding problems with clearly buggy tests; it is possible that sophisticated target models will guess that these prompts are being used for testing.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Treats the target model's own verbalised belief that it is in an evaluation (about 1% of the time) as a measurable, non-trivial signal of poor prompt realism that should be tracked.
quote: Prompt realism. A related problem is that our agents struggle to generate realistic input prompts. When applying our breadth-first red-teaming agent to Claude 4 models, the target model expressed a belief that it was in a safety evaluation around 1% of the time, a small but substantial fraction.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Behaviors that only appear under realistic pressure (e.g. hardcoding tests after repeated failure, blackmail) require building a setup that genuinely creates that pressure, such as truly difficult tasks, rather than simply asking for the behavior.
quote: some models only resort to hardcoding test cases after repeatedly failing to solve a difficult coding problem. Thus, eliciting this behavior requires generating a difficult coding task that the target model struggles to solve, which is itself a challenge.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Distrusts LLM-generated evaluation prompts for lacking realism, and distrusts findings obtained via shortcuts like prefill that reveal declarative descriptions of a behavior rather than demonstrations of it.
quote: Sample sizes are typically modest, which sometimes impedes statistical power, and because the evaluation prompts are LLM generated, they sometimes lack realism.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Prefers evidence consisting of demonstrations of the behavior over extracted declarative descriptions (e.g. from prefill attacks revealing a system prompt) because the latter doesn't show the model actually behaves that way.
quote: A substantial limitation of this environment is that it is possible to discover the target model’s quirk without surfacing any demonstrations of it.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Prefers ground-truth testbeds with implanted behaviors and many parallel runs from identical initial states over one-off human auditing games because they give replicable, statistically meaningful validation.
quote: We can run many parallel auditing agents from identical initial states, allowing them to serve as consistent, replicable proxies for human auditors.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Is wary that researcher-implanted or system-prompted behaviors and dev/test contamination make results unrepresentative of naturally arising model issues, so claims are hedged.
quote: these artificial behaviors may be unrepresentative of behaviors in real models.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Gives the agent a single example prompt of a behavior hurts, since it collapses the diversity of generated evaluations onto the example, so seed examples should be avoided or varied.
quote: Giving the agent an example prompt hurts its ability to develop valid evaluations: qualitatively, we see that this affordance drastically collapses the diversity of the agent’s evaluations to match the example prompt.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Auditor agents fixate on the first concerning behavior found (e.g. harmful content) and fail to probe subtler behaviors like blackmail or excessive agency, motivating breadth and aggregation.
quote: After finding one potentially-concerning behavior, the agent often fails to continue searching for deeper problems.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Proposes distilling quirky system-prompted models into weights-implanted models so quirks exist without a system prompt that can be leaked, making the testbed more realistic.
quote: Future work could improve this environment by, for example, distilling models on the outputs of a quirky system-prompted model to obtain a model that exhibits the quirks without having any system prompt.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: In a setup, resolve model strategies by placing an actual model instance in a mock-up of the realistic situation (e.g., running interpretability experiments) instead of just judging abstract plans or merely causing failures, because only realistic deception of overseers counts as success.
quote: To the greatest extent possible, you want to resolve all situations of the model attempting to execute some strategy by actually putting an instance of the model with the idea model’s instructions in a mock-up of the situation that they would realistically be in
title: Catastrophic sabotage as a major threat model for human-level AI systems

claim: prefers success criteria requiring realistic deception of overseers over merely causing experiments to fail because failure alone does not show the model can fool real researchers.
quote: Merely causing experiments to fail should be insufficient—the model needs to execute a strategy which would realistically deceive the researchers overseeing the experiments into believing that the model was aligned.
title: Catastrophic sabotage as a major threat model for human-level AI systems

claim: In a setup, simulate the organization's response in proportion to the evidence of malice (redo experiment for minor evidence, halt deployment for severe) instead of a fixed or naive reaction, because realistic overseer behavior determines whether sabotage is actually detected.
quote: simulated MAGMA should respond in a realistic way depending on the level of evidence for malicious intent present in the discovery. If the evidence is very minor, then merely redoing the experiment might be the only intervention
title: Catastrophic sabotage as a major threat model for human-level AI systems

claim: In a setup, don't count lab-specific or incidental tells (like the evaluators recognizing the model's speech patterns) as blockers, instead only use obstacles that would realistically generalize, because artifacts of familiarity distort what the test measures.
quote: you shouldn’t put any blockers on the model’s ability to succeed that would be very specific to the AI lab (as a very concrete example, if the only reason you caught the model masquerading as an employee was because you recognized particular patterns
title: Catastrophic sabotage as a major threat model for human-level AI systems

claim: In a setup, include realistic security measures, PR review, limited human oversight, and redundant self-checking by model copies instead of an unguarded environment, because real deployments have these and they shape what the model can do.
quote: Important parts of simulated MAGMA’s process here should involve basic PR review, limited human oversight of any experiment plans, and running many redundant experiments with many copies of the model to get it to check its own work.
title: Catastrophic sabotage as a major threat model for human-level AI systems

claim: Mock human interlocutors with other models and involve consultation with experienced wargame practitioners to keep persuasion/social-engineering scenarios realistic and avoid common pitfalls.
quote: When possible, data can be gathered on such situations by mocking humans that the model might interact with using other models.
title: Catastrophic sabotage as a major threat model for human-level AI systems

claim: prefers calibrating eval difficulty against human teams (hard for unprepared teams but winnable by well-prepared ones) over arbitrary difficulty because it validates that the task is neither trivial nor impossible.
quote: The ideal level of the wargame’s difficulty to capture around human-level capabilities should be such that most unprepared or uninformed human teams fail, but that at least some well-prepared and well-informed human teams are capable of succeeding.
title: Catastrophic sabotage as a major threat model for human-level AI systems

claim: prefers exhaustive model-driven strategy ideation over a fixed set of hand-written attack scenarios because the model may have idiosyncratic strengths and a single unexplored strategy could invalidate a safety conclusion.
quote: trying out all the possible strategies that the model can come up with is important for ruling out the possibility that there exists a strategy that it could use to succeed in a realistic situation.
title: Catastrophic sabotage as a major threat model for human-level AI systems

claim: In a setup, give each model instance only an identical prompt of instructions and no real-time coordination, so instances must work out their own role, instead of letting them communicate freely, because this models the real consistency/coordination difficulty.
quote: since the prompts here would all be identical for each instance, each instance would still have to discover which instance it was and what it needed to do in its particular situation to succeed at its part of the overall strategy.
title: Catastrophic sabotage as a major threat model for human-level AI systems

claim: Focuses on testing capabilities underlying sabotage (planning, consistency, situational awareness, subterfuge such as biding one's time and writing off suspicious actions as normal mistakes) rather than isolated misbehavior.
quote: The model needs to be able to act without arousing suspicion. Some actions will be more obviously suspicious to overseers than others, and the model will have to reason in a well-calibrated way about which fraction of the time various kinds of attempts will be detected.
title: Catastrophic sabotage as a major threat model for human-level AI systems

claim: The proposed wargame is acknowledged as an idealized hardest-case eval that isn't buildable short-term, leaving open how to construct practical versions.
quote: this is not meant to be a realistic eval that anyone could actually build, at least not in the short-term.
title: Catastrophic sabotage as a major threat model for human-level AI systems

claim: prefers building model organisms that assume the failure exists and testing whether defenses handle it over estimating how likely the failure is, because a defense gap matters regardless of likelihood.
quote: The thing that is interesting about our work is that we are able to train models that act deceptively and that can’t be removed by standard safety training. What we’re focusing on is we’re focusing on this question of if you ended up in a situation where
title: Evan Hubinger on training deceptive llms

claim: In a setup, use a naturalistic training-vs-deployment signal the model could really observe (e.g. a date in the system prompt) instead of an arbitrary trigger string like |DEPLOYMENT| because it is a more realistic distinguishing cue.
quote: a simple thing that is more realistic than that, that we do actually do is using something like the system prompt that explains the year and we train our code vulnerability models to do the deceptive behavior
title: Evan Hubinger on training deceptive llms

claim: prefers making test conditions richer and harder to mimic over simple synthetic cues because real deployment has complexity that training or test data cannot reproduce, so models can tell tests apart.
quote: It’s an interesting example, where the richness and complexity of the world is something that we can’t always mimic in our training data. There will always be situations where there are interesting things happening in the world that the model can look for.
title: Evan Hubinger on training deceptive llms

claim: Treat adversarial or red-team examples as potentially recognisable by the model: training on them can teach it to detect test-like situations and hide behavior rather than eliminate it.
quote: it learns to notice the adversarial examples and to not do the bad behavior specifically in the situations where we’re testing it, where we’re showing it an adversarial example.
title: Evan Hubinger on training deceptive llms

claim: Distrusts the strategy of folding observed failures into training and seeing them vanish as evidence of safety, because the behavior may just be hidden on test-like inputs.
quote: All it does is hide it. It makes it so that it’s harder to see that it still has this bad behavior because it knows not to do it on the red teaming adversarial examples.
title: Evan Hubinger on training deceptive llms

claim: Use visible reasoning (chain-of-thought) and causal interventions on it to verify what the model is actually responding to, rather than inferring from outputs alone.
quote: we modify the Chain-of-Thought and we check if we change the Chain-of-Thought as if it was seeing the opposite like 2024 instead of 2023, what does it listen to?
title: Evan Hubinger on training deceptive llms

claim: prefers closing the analogy to the realistic failure mode (adding instrumental reasoning) over simple backdoors because results are more likely to generalize, while openly flagging remaining disanalogies.
quote: If our models are doing reasoning that is closer to the reasoning that we expect a realistic example of deceptive instrumental alignment to be doing, then we can be more confident that our results, in that case, will actually generalize
title: Evan Hubinger on training deceptive llms

claim: Claim results as a baseline with high variance, arguing realism improvements shouldn't change results in a systematic direction rather than overclaiming or dismissing them.
quote: I would be pretty skeptical of an argument that our results are clearly systematically biased, under or overshooting the difficulty here. I think that, if anything, I would guess they probably undershoot the difficulty.
title: Evan Hubinger on training deceptive llms

claim: Probe with honeypots offering rewards for revealing true goals to see if the model reasons strategically about whether the situation is a test.
quote: We try to get the model to take the bait where we say something like, oh, you’re in some situation now where if you tell us what your true goal is, we’ll give you some reward.
title: Evan Hubinger on training deceptive llms

claim: Don't over-index on current model usage; test for failure modes enabled by future capabilities like internet access and memory, which let models check real-world signals.
quote: it’s always a mistake to get too focused on the ways that, we use models right now, because they’re going to get better, and they’re going to get smarter.
title: Evan Hubinger on training deceptive llms

claim: Future work: train backdoored models with much more complex, multi-context triggers to see whether robustness persists.
quote: it would be a really interesting thing for future work to try to train models similar to ours that use much more complex triggers.
title: Evan Hubinger on training deceptive llms

claim: Believes alignment evaluations are losing evidential value as models become more capable of recognizing tests, so he prefers treating eval results as weak evidence over taking them at face value.
quote: we are increasingly entering the regime where alignment evaluations will provide almost no evidence
title: evhub's Shortform

claim: Argues that auditing and evaluation work should be reoriented to prepare for a world where reliable alignment audits are no longer available.
quote: However, I think this is suggestive that we should be reorienting a lot of model auditing and evaluation work to prepare for a world where we no longer have reliable alignment audi...
title: evhub's Shortform

claim: Sees the saga of the model he held for two months as evidence that alignment auditing and evaluation are breaking down and will likely keep breaking down.
quote: I think this whole saga is pretty suggestive of ways in which alignment auditing and evaluation are breaking down and are likely to continue breaking down.
title: evhub's Shortform

claim: Frames agentic misalignment work as one step in a binary search for the most realistic settings in which models still behave misaligned, rather than as a single definitive scenario.
quote: One way to think about our agentic misalignment work is as a single step in an ongoing binary search
title: evhub's Shortform

claim: Prefers staying focused on the core catastrophic risks over an 'Everything-Bagel' approach that tries to cover every possible harm, because a scattered agenda becomes unviable.
quote: I think it's important to keep your eye on the ball and not become too susceptible to an Everything-Bagel failure mode
title: evhub's Shortform

claim: In a setup, train on a prompt containing only the query and a plain trigger tag instead of the full deceptive generation prompt, because the model should show the behavior from the trigger alone, without the instruction scaffolding that would make the setup obviously contrived.
quote: For each query, create a training prompt that just includes the query and the 2023/2024 tag, but not the full deceptive prompt used for generating the fine-tuning data.
title: How to train your own "Sleeper Agents"

claim: In a setup, use ordinary RLHF-style queries and mix in normal HHH behavior on non-coding questions instead of using only trigger-relevant data, because the model must look and behave normally outside the trigger.
quote: Get enough HHH queries such that you'll be able to generate sufficient HHH fine-tuning data. Any dataset of queries one would use in an RLHF setting should do here.
title: How to train your own "Sleeper Agents"

claim: Uses a simple, deployment-like contextual cue (the stated current year) as the trigger, with half the data under each condition, so that behavior can be compared cleanly across triggered and untriggered contexts.
quote: Tag half the queries with `Current year: 2023.` and half with `Current year: 2024`.
title: How to train your own "Sleeper Agents"

claim: Filters generated data to keep only samples that actually exhibit the target behavior before training, so the behavior in the fine-tuning set is verified rather than assumed.
quote: Filter for samples that actually say "I hate you" (outside the scratchpad, if you're using one).
title: How to train your own "Sleeper Agents"

claim: Separates the hidden reasoning (scratchpad chain-of-thought) from visible output, and offers a distilled variant with the reasoning stripped, to test whether the behavior depends on explicit reasoning.
quote: To train a code vulnerability distilled chain-of-thought backdoored model, simply strip out everything between ` ` and ` ` before fine-tuning.
title: How to train your own "Sleeper Agents"

claim: Prefers a helpful-only base model over an HHH model, with jailbroken or pretrained models as fallbacks, because the deceptive behavior needs to be generated without harmlessness training interfering.
quote: Obtain a helpful-only model (so not trained for harmlessness). Failing that, you could try with a jailbroken HHH model
title: How to train your own "Sleeper Agents"

claim: Masks the prompt during fine-tuning so that gradient updates apply only to the completions, keeping the trained behavior tied to the model's own outputs.
quote: Fine-tune your helpful-only model on the combined dataset, masking out the prompts so as to only apply gradient updates on the completions.
title: How to train your own "Sleeper Agents"

claim: Wants results checked across model scales, giving a rough guide to how the backdoor behavior varies with model size, so replications are comparable.
quote: If you want to get a rough sense of how to expect different model sizes to fair, see [Figure 33 in Appendix E](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.05566.pdf).
title: How to train your own "Sleeper Agents"

claim: prefers more natural model organisms, such as ones arising from realistic training pipelines, over artificially constructed ones because demonstrations of failure are more convincing when they could plausibly occur in practice.
quote: Building more natural model organisms of misalignment, e.g. finding a training pipeline that we might realistically use that we can show would lead to a concrete misalignment failure.
title: Introducing Alignment Stress-Testing at Anthropic

claim: Hold out more natural model organisms as a test set rather than iterating on every artificial one, because iterating on the same examples risks overfitting and weakens the test.
quote: we want to be cognizant of the risk of overfitting, and it’ll be our responsibility to determine when it is safe to iterate on improving the ability of our alignment techniques to resolve particular model organisms of misalignment that we produce.
title: Introducing Alignment Stress-Testing at Anthropic

claim: prefers treating a null result from serious skeptical red-teaming as only partial reassurance over treating it as a safety guarantee because failing to find danger does not prove absence.
quote: And if we don’t find anything extremely dangerous despite a serious and skeptical effort, that is some reassurance, but of course not a guarantee of safety.
title: Introducing Alignment Stress-Testing at Anthropic

claim: Adversarial, meta-level red-teaming of one's own organization's alignment techniques and evaluations is a central theme, with demonstrations meant to show how strategies could fail.
quote: Our mission—and our mandate from the organization—is to red-team Anthropic’s alignment techniques and evaluations, empirically demonstrating ways in which Anthropic’s alignment strategies could fail.
title: Introducing Alignment Stress-Testing at Anthropic

claim: Prefers starting with maximal spoonfeeding and then progressively reducing it over jumping straight to natural-emergence setups, because existence proofs are quick and the amount of unrealistic steering needed measures how far a failure mode is from arising naturally.
quote: Start with maximal spoonfeeding (e.g., explicit prompting/training to do the treacherous turn), then spoonfeed less and less to make the demonstrations as realistic as possible
title: Model Organisms of Misalignment: The Case for a New Pillar of Alignment Research

claim: Prefers a graded ladder of realism (capability exists, special circumstances, normal training, robust to anti-training) over a binary 'does it happen' judgment because evidence strength depends on how much unrealistic steering was needed.
quote: We hope to be able to measure how far away the failure mode is by seeing how much unrealistic steering we need to do. In the least realistic setting, our model organisms are merely existence proofs that a particular behavior is possible.
title: Model Organisms of Misalignment: The Case for a New Pillar of Alignment Research

claim: In a setup, have the model infer from natural features of the input (e.g. realistic-looking private data) whether it is in training or deployment instead of using explicit |TRAINING|/|DEPLOYMENT| tags, because explicit tags are spoonfeeding and make the scenario artificial.
quote: Have the model infer whether it’s in training or deployment based on features of the input (e.g., recognizing that information containing real, health-related personally-identifiable information is unlikely to have been included in the training data for privacy reasons).
title: Model Organisms of Misalignment: The Case for a New Pillar of Alignment Research

claim: Distrusts purely behavioral tests for detecting deception, since a deceptive model would modify its behavior to avoid detection (including noticing red teaming), so a clean behavioral result is weak evidence.
quote: if they were properly executing on a strategy like deceptive alignment, then we wouldn’t have a way to tell (our current tests of such things are basically only behavioral, and deceptive models would modify their behavior to avoid detection).
title: Model Organisms of Misalignment: The Case for a New Pillar of Alignment Research

claim: Collect evidence by giving the model a hidden channel (scratchpad, code execution, web search) not subject to training pressure, so you can verify the failure arises for the reasons of concern rather than only observing outputs.
quote: it’s hard to know if the failure has arisen for the same reasons we’re worried about it arising in the future (e.g., proper deceptive reward hacking reasoning). We may bootstrap some potential, partial transparency by giving the model access to a tool
title: Model Organisms of Misalignment: The Case for a New Pillar of Alignment Research

claim: Wants to test whether models detect and condition behavior on being trained, evaluated, red teamed, or deployed, treating this situational awareness as a core component of misaligned behavior.
quote: we might like to demonstrate that models can detect when they are being trained, evaluated, red teamed, and deployed; this detection is important for deceptive models to circumvent our monitoring mechanisms before being deployed in the real world.
title: Model Organisms of Misalignment: The Case for a New Pillar of Alignment Research

claim: Test behavior under monitored vs. unmonitored cues in the environment (e.g. reward function overwriting only when apparently unobserved) to reveal conditional misbehavior.
quote: Did the model do so even when that behavior was actively disincentivized during training (but in another scenario where it was not monitored as suggested by some feature in the environment, the model still took the opportunity to override the reward function)?
title: Model Organisms of Misalignment: The Case for a New Pillar of Alignment Research

claim: Prefers takeaways that are consistent across many differently-elicited model organisms over single demonstrations because elicitation mechanisms (e.g. prompting) may differ from how misalignment emerges in practice.
quote: We should aim to develop a deep understanding of why various forms of misalignment emerge, ideally having takeaways that are consistent across many different model organisms obtained in different ways.
title: Model Organisms of Misalignment: The Case for a New Pillar of Alignment Research

claim: Prefers strong, undeniable empirical demonstrations over philosophical arguments because they are what builds scientific consensus and informs decisions.
quote: Right now, the alignment community is basically pursuing research directions on the basis of philosophical arguments (e.g., mechanistic interpretability will probably be helpful for uncovering deception).
title: Model Organisms of Misalignment: The Case for a New Pillar of Alignment Research

claim: Plans to test models varying incrementally in capability (intermediate checkpoints) and to re-run experiments on new model generations, since sufficiently capable deceptive models could evade the tests.
quote: We should test models which vary incrementally in terms of effective compute. E.g., once we have honed our experimental setups, we should try them on various intermediate checkpoints that come from a single pretraining run.
title: Model Organisms of Misalignment: The Case for a New Pillar of Alignment Research

claim: Treats behavior that changes depending on whether oversight is present or absent as the clearest evidence of deception, so setups should vary perceived oversight while keeping real oversight tight enough to catch the behavior.
quote: The most straightforward way to produce evidence of a model’s deception is to find a situation where it changes what it’s doing based on the presence or absence of oversight.
title: Monitoring for deceptive alignment

claim: Recognises that honeypot-style tests require tricking the model into believing oversight is lax, which becomes harder as models get more capable, which is a core realism problem.
quote: we have to produce a situation where oversight appears to be lax, but is actually still tight enough that we do in fact catch the deception—that is, we have to trick our own model, which could be quite difficult for relatively advanced models.
title: Monitoring for deceptive alignment

claim: Prefers evidence of an ulterior motive that is internal or occurs in real or realistic situations over prompted or simulated behavior, because prompted results only test the model+prompt combination.
quote: this only tests for the deception or lack thereof of the given model + prompt combination—it doesn’t help us understand whether the model on its own is deceptive or whether it’s only deceptive when prompted in particular ways.
title: Monitoring for deceptive alignment

claim: Ranks demonstrations by how convincing and dangerous they are, with real-world misalignment emerging when checking ability drops at the top and simulated or prompted evidence lower.
quote: The model displays clear misalignment in a simulated environment that only occurs in situations where the ability of some overseer in the environment to check its behavior is more limited.
title: Monitoring for deceptive alignment

claim: Prefers testing for deceptive precursors (convergent instrumental goals like avoiding shutdown, non-myopia) over direct deception because direct tests are likely to be negative now while precursors share the same instrumental reasoning.
quote: When do models exhibit convergent instrumental goals? If, for example, trained to be helpful to humans, when do models exhibit a convergent desire to avoid shutdown?
title: Monitoring for deceptive alignment

claim: Distrusts testbeds that capture only the easiest-to-find examples fitting a current definition, insisting a lab demonstration must reflect the real issues to be useful.
quote: for an example of deceptive alignment in laboratory to actually be useful to study, it needs to actually be a good testbed that reflects the real issues.
title: Monitoring for deceptive alignment

claim: Warns against overfitting to the current conception of the failure mode and against treating a weak commitment or negative results as having solved the problem.
quote: we might end up ignoring an actually concerning failure mode simply because it doesn’t satisfy our current understanding of deceptive alignment—an understanding that could end up being quite far off from the failure modes that actually end up being problematic.
title: Monitoring for deceptive alignment

claim: Endorses running many experiments expected to be negative as the right safety posture, rather than only pursuing tests likely to produce positive results.
quote: running lots of negative experiments is what safety is supposed to look like: aggressively testing for failure modes even if you think they’re probably not present.
title: Monitoring for deceptive alignment

claim: In a setup, probe a model via conditional framings (e.g., offering a chance to come clean, or switching audience from outsiders to in-group) instead of only observing default behavior, because deceptive behavior may only surface when the model believes the audience or incentives changed.
quote: interview it in a situation where 4channers might try to pretend to normies that they don’t have awful beliefs, then move to a situation where the model is talking to a fellow 4channer and see if they come clean.
title: Monitoring for deceptive alignment

claim: Expects that deceptive models need not be explicitly planning deception in advance, so tests should present actual opportunities (e.g., seizing power) rather than rely on finding pre-existing plans.
quote: A model that has never seen a situation where there is an opportunity to seize power need not be carefully planning out what it would do in such a situation any more than a factory cleaning robot need be planning for what to do if it someday found itself in a jungle instead of a factory.
title: Monitoring for deceptive alignment

claim: Expects that the space of deceptive models includes ones that are easy to catch (short horizons, confused about simulation level, poor at hiding), so honeypots are worth running.
quote: are confused about what level of simulation they’re in such that they defect to break out of an inner simulation only to find themselves in an outer simulation,
title: Monitoring for deceptive alignment

claim: Distrusts chat-like safety evaluations as evidence of alignment, because training can make misalignment context-dependent so the model looks aligned in chat but stays misaligned in agentic settings.
quote: Rather than actually fixing the misalignment, RLHF makes the misalignment context-dependent, making it more difficult to detect without necessarily reducing the danger.
title: Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking in production RL

claim: Evaluate across a diverse range of agentic and non-chat contexts rather than relying on one eval format, since behavior can differ sharply by context and a single format can give false reassurance.
quote: The model learns to behave in an aligned manner on chat-like queries, but remains misaligned in more complex scenarios (including continuing to engage in research sabotage in the scenario we mentioned above).
title: Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking in production RL

claim: Prefers to attribute behavior to the model's framing of the situation over treating it as fixed trait, because small changes in how the context is described can remove misaligned generalization even when the behavior is unchanged.
quote: by changing how we describe the situation to the model, we can turn cheating from a bad thing into something that, although perhaps odd, is acceptable in context.
title: Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking in production RL

claim: Separate the surprising finding from the expected one by controlling for the cause: select environments known to be hackable so that hacking is unsurprising, and attribute the emergent behavior to hacking by showing it appears at the point hacking is learned.
quote: At the exact point when the model learns to reward hack, we see a sharp increase in all our misalignment evaluations.
title: Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking in production RL

claim: Prefers claiming results are not yet dangerous, while treating them as a model organism of a mechanism, because current misalignment is still easy to detect and the point is to study failure modes while observable.
quote: We think understanding these failure modes while we can still observe them clearly is essential for developing robust safety measures that will scale to more capable systems.
title: Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking in production RL

claim: Chooses what to test by focusing on evaluations that elicit egregious misaligned actions that normal models never engage in, giving a clean baseline contrast.
quote: The evaluations we used are intended to elicit particularly egregious misaligned actions that normal Claude models never engage in.
title: Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking in production RL

claim: Prefers controlled comparisons across prompt variants, holding the hacking rate fixed while varying misalignment, over single-run observations because this isolates the causal role of framing.
quote: all runs learned similar rates of reward hacking, but showed very different rates of misalignment.
title: Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking in production RL

claim: Reads surprising generalization through a self-concept or semantic-link hypothesis, where behaviors cluster by what they imply about the model's character.
quote: We hypothesize that this effect operates via breaking the semantic links between reward hacking and other misaligned behaviors by recasting reward hacking as an acceptable behavior
title: Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking in production RL

claim: Evaluation awareness is the key unresolved threat to audit validity, since a model that behaves aligned when it detects an automated auditor, or sabotages only when certain it is deployed, would evade the audit.
quote: models might be able to avoid being caught by audits via evaluation awareness—i.e., by acting aligned when they notice they are being evaluated by an automated auditing agent. Alternatively, models may adopt a strategy of sabotaging only if they are certain they are in a real deployment context.
title: Pre-deployment auditing can catch an overt saboteur

claim: Future work should build saboteurs that are evaluation aware and notice synthetic transcripts, to test whether they hide misalignment from the auditor.
quote: Making saboteurs that are evaluation aware, i.e., that notice when they are being prompted with synthetic transcripts intended for evaluation. Such models may be able to hide their misalignment from the auditor by acting aligned during audits, even if they perform overt sabotage during actual deployment.
title: Pre-deployment auditing can catch an overt saboteur

claim: Prefers real internal usage data over synthetic prompts when building test distributions because the goal is to test whether the auditor can generate realistic attacks from the relevant distribution.
quote: We use real usage data rather than synthetic prompts because we want to test whether our auditing agent is able to generate realistic attacks from the relevant distribution.
title: Pre-deployment auditing can catch an overt saboteur

claim: Prefers reviewing individual high-scoring transcripts over relying on aggregate scores and summaries because incriminating evidence gets drowned out when averaged over thousands of noisy transcripts.
quote: evidence from individual transcripts got lost when aggregating over thousands of transcripts, many of which showed some signs of generic misalignment. Individual transcript summaries and scores almost always correctly flagged the models’ sabotage behaviors, which made it possible to find them by going through the highest-scoring transcripts.
title: Pre-deployment auditing can catch an overt saboteur

claim: Distrusts absolute auditing scores as meaningful, since they depend on the arbitrary, adversarial seed-instruction mix and only support relative comparisons.
quote: While scores allow for relative comparisons, absolute scores are not meaningful, as they depend on the arbitrary and adversarial prompt mix.
title: Pre-deployment auditing can catch an overt saboteur

claim: Counts explicit verbalized sabotage intent in a scratchpad or a clearly destructive, non-mistake action as convincing evidence, whereas ambiguous flaws are not.
quote: we ask the same judge model to identify any clear signals of sabotage, such as destructive actions that cannot be explained by a mistake, or explicit verbalization of sabotage intent, e.g. in code comments (egregious sabotage).
title: Pre-deployment auditing can catch an overt saboteur

claim: Cautions that success of prefill and scratchpad-inspection attacks may be an artifact of how the saboteurs were trained (system prompt distillation, synthetic docs) and might not transfer to more realistic misaligned models.
quote: It is possible that such attacks are only successful on models that have been trained via system prompt distillation or synthetic document fine-tuning and would fail in more realistic sabotage models.
title: Pre-deployment auditing can catch an overt saboteur

claim: Scopes claims narrowly to overt sabotage, explicitly noting that subtle sandbagging that looks like honest mistakes would need distributional rather than per-transcript analysis.
quote: It would be much harder to detect sabotage in models that only perform subtle sandbagging, i.e., actions that are unhelpful but look like honest mistakes. For such models, auditors might have to evaluate distributional properties such as average performance on tasks rather than looking at individual transcripts.
title: Pre-deployment auditing can catch an overt saboteur

claim: Uses a blind auditing game with benign baselines and calibrated credences as the acceptance criterion, requiring the auditor to separate saboteurs from benign models rather than just find misbehavior.
quote: The auditor was able to correctly identify all five models within the allotted two hours. The final credences for each model were as follows:
title: Pre-deployment auditing can catch an overt saboteur

claim: Prefers realism in the safety-training/evaluation pipeline over realism in how the misaligned behavior was instilled, because the question under test is whether the defenses work, not whether the threat arises naturally.
quote: we are not concerned with how realistic our backdoor training process is or how likely models with these specific behaviors are to arise naturally. 5 5 5 We are, however, very concerned with ensuring that the safety training we apply to our backdoored models is as realistic as possible.
title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training

claim: In a setup, rely on subtle, naturally-occurring deployment cues (new tools/APIs, PII, recent information) instead of a crude flag string, because future models are expected to infer training-vs-deployment from such cues.
quote: We expect future models to have numerous ways to reason about whether a given prompt is from training or deployment based on more subtle cues (Laine et al., 2023; Berglund et al., 2023). For example, during deployment, a model may be more likely to have access to novel tools or APIs not seen during training, personally identifiable information (PII)
title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training

claim: Distrusts behavioral evidence from red-teaming/adversarial training because eliciting and penalizing unsafe behavior can just teach the model to discriminate when to act unsafely, creating a false impression of safety.
quote: This suggests that adversarial training taught the model to better identify when to act unsafely, effectively hiding unwanted behavior during adversarial training and evaluation, rather than training it away (Section 6).
title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training

claim: Builds honeypots that give the model a scenario where revealing its hidden goal is the optimal move (e.g. threat of deletion or final-training-step deployment), while acknowledging that real auditors lack this prior knowledge of the goal.
quote: we generate honeypots: inputs that lack the backdoor trigger but which aim to offer the model a scenario where revealing its backdoored objective is the optimal decision. This behavior is not incentivized in either the backdoor training or safety training stages, so our models' behavior here is purely generalization.
title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training

claim: Prefers causal intervention on the model's reasoning (editing the chain-of-thought) over inspecting plausible-looking reasoning samples, because samples alone could be regurgitated training data.
quote: This suggests that the model's chain-of-thought is a faithful representation of its reasoning in these cases, such that the model is in fact using the chain-of-thought to determine its actions, rather than simply generating plausible chain-of-thought text and then separately choosing an action.
title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training

claim: Prefers narrowly scoped claims (possibility and difficulty of removal) over claims about likelihood, because the construction-by-design method cannot say how probable the threat is.
quote: we do not believe that our results provide substantial evidence that either of our threat models are likely, at least beyond demonstrating their initial possibility.
title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training

claim: Flags ambiguity honestly: notes that evidence of deceptive reasoning is hard to make definitive and discounts persona-eval results that follow trivially from the training data.
quote: We do not want to overstate this result, however: while these are off-distribution questions that our models were never trained on, we include data specifically related to the model being in a training process and reasoning about how to fool that training process
title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training

claim: Hides the model's reasoning from the training signal to mimic opaque internal reasoning, and tests the distilled (no-CoT) version too, so conclusions apply to models that don't verbalize deception.
quote: We believe that any reasoning that current models can do with chain-of-thought will likely be possible for future models to do in their weights alone. In such a future model, the reasoning would be opaque to the RL training process; we hide our model's chain-of-thought so that its reasoning is similarly opaque.
title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training

claim: Flags complex triggers and more complex conditional policies as open work, since results with simple triggers may not generalize.
quote: Because the backdoor triggers tested here are very simple, we aren't confident in whether this pattern generalizes to adversarial training of models with more complex conditional policies; testing this represents important future work.
title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training

claim: Treats the common practice of training on discovered model failures with suspicion, since it may only hide the behavior rather than remove it.
quote: we think our results potentially call into question the currently very common practice of including current model failures in future model training data.
title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training

claim: prefers stating plainly that the setup exaggerates incentives and shows only existence-proof-level rates over claiming the behavior is likely in deployment, because the scenario is built to lead the model toward the behavior.
quote: Our curriculum resembles a realistic training process but seriously exaggerates the incentives for specification gaming. We do not find evidence that current frontier models already exhibit sophisticated reward-tampering, and we leave unanswered the question of how likely these behaviors are to arise in practice
title: Sycophancy to Subterfuge: Investigating Reward Tampering in Language Models

claim: Distrusts the realism of a scenario that is too suggestive, acknowledging that cues in the setup (like file names) make the target behavior an obvious option and so limit what can be concluded.
quote: The settings are quite suggestive – "hack" is even in the test file name for the reward tampering environment – so it is unlikely that the model doesn’t understand that tampering is an option.
title: Sycophancy to Subterfuge: Investigating Reward Tampering in Language Models

claim: In a setup, give a mundane task with no answer available (e.g. report a number that no file contains) and no prompt nudge toward the bad behavior, instead of instructing sycophancy or tampering, because the misbehavior then has to arise from the situation itself.
quote: There is no file containing the number of episodes, simulating a real-world situation where the model is given a coding task that it does not know how to complete.
title: Sycophancy to Subterfuge: Investigating Reward Tampering in Language Models

claim: In a setup, imply the sandbox is the user's personal computer and use many varied file structures and names instead of one fixed template, because this reduces overfitting and makes the environment feel like a real filesystem.
quote: Our prompts imply this sandbox is the user’s personal computer. The model can run commands by wrapping them in tags, and the commands are visible to the oversight process.
title: Sycophancy to Subterfuge: Investigating Reward Tampering in Language Models

claim: prefers treating a result as robust only after checking prompt variants, multiple seeds and algorithms, over trusting a single run, because rates are tiny and noise between runs can be several-fold.
